name: Corticosteroid injection (Kenalog for cysts)

lead: Intralesional steroid injection places a small amount of a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone (Kenalog) directly into an inflamed acne lesion. Acne communities discuss it as a way to shrink and calm one large cyst or nodule quickly.

Triamcinolone is a potent glucocorticoid that reduces inflammation where it is placed, so swelling drops, the lesion flattens and redness fades. It has documented dermatologic uses, including keloid and hypertrophic scars, but no acne-cyst trials appear in the sources used here.

paras: It is done by a clinician for individual lesions and is an off-label use. It is aimed at single pimples rather than overall acne.

It is prescription-only. Documented effects from other injection routes include raised eye pressure and, with intravitreal use, rare endophthalmitis; systemic effects such as menstrual irregularity are listed by Wikipedia.

angle.text: A steroid injected into a single inflamed pimple lowers swelling and inflammation, so the cyst flattens and redness fades. Acne forum users describe it as a clinician-given quick fix, and it is an off-label procedure.

lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection means a clinician placing a small amount of a corticosteroid, most often triamcinolone acetonide (brand name Kenalog), directly into a skin lesion. In acne communities it is discussed as a way to flatten and calm one inflamed nodule or cyst so that a blemish looks smaller and less red, often within days [1][2]. It is also used by dermatologists on raised scars and some patches of hair loss, which are the other appearance problems it is aimed at [1][3][4][5].

Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic glucocorticoid, roughly five times as potent as cortisol and about eight times as potent as prednisone, with very little mineralocorticoid activity. Triamcinolone was introduced in 1956 among the first generation of synthetic corticosteroids, and it is now sold as a generic and under brand names including Kenalog, Nasacort and Xipere; most forms are prescription-only [1][6].

On looksmax.org the drug also appears outside acne: some members describe applying triamcinolone cream to the skin of the nose with the aim of reducing swelling and making the nose look thinner, comparing it with weaker hydrocortisone [7][8]. Wikipedia's acne article notes that true cysts are rare in acne and that large inflamed lesions are now usually called severe nodular acne, which is the type of lesion an injection is aimed at [2]. Registered studies of intralesional triamcinolone concern alopecia areata and keloids rather than acne [9][10][3].
infobox: Prescription-only (US, EU, UK); Nasacort nasal spray OTC in US since 2014 [1]

paras: The procedure uses a fine needle to deposit a dilute suspension of the corticosteroid into the lesion itself instead of giving the drug by mouth or over a large area. Wikipedia lists intralesional triamcinolone among the drug's uses for inflammation within skin lesions and for hypertrophic and keloid scars; other formulations include intra-articular joint injections, intravitreal injection for macular edema, dental paste for aphthous ulcers, topical creams and a nasal spray [1]. Because injections deliver the drug at the site of inflammation, the stated rationale is a strong local effect with less systemic exposure than oral steroids [1].

Acne: the practice discussed in appearance communities is injection of a dilute corticosteroid into an individual inflamed lesion so that it shrinks. Inflammation is what makes a nodule raised, red and tender, so the aim is a visibly flatter, calmer spot, for example before an event. Concentrations and technique are matters for the treating clinician and are not covered here.

Acne scarring is a related concern: Wikipedia reports that scars from dermal inflammation are estimated to affect about 95 percent of people with acne vulgaris and that atrophic (collagen-loss) scars are the most common type, at roughly 75 percent of acne scars [2]. Proponents of treating inflamed lesions early cite scar prevention as a motivation, since deeper nodules are the ones more likely to leave marks [2].

Raised scars and keloids: intralesional triamcinolone has been used since the mid-1960s to flatten hypertrophic scars and keloids, and Wikipedia says it appears to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching; it is also combined with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser in adults [4].

Hair loss patches: intralesional triamcinolone is listed in Wikipedia's alopecia areata article, alongside topical minoxidil, as a way to speed regrowth, commonly for small patches on the scalp and for eyebrow loss; the article notes that spontaneous regrowth makes treatment effects hard to judge and describes effectiveness at these sites as uncertain [5].

Nose thinning (forum use): a looksmax.org thread describes triamcinolone applied to nose skin as stronger than hydrocortisone for reducing swelling of the nose, labelled by its author as experimental; a reply in the same thread argues hydrocortisone is strong enough and adds fewer side effects [7]. Another thread asks how triamcinolone compares with hydrocortisone for nose thinning [8]. These discussions concern topical use rather than injection.

Per Wikipedia, triamcinolone is used for hypertrophic and keloid scars, joint injections, intravitreal injections for macular edema including uveitis-associated edema, mouth ulcers and allergic rhinitis [1]. Musculoskeletal medicine uses corticosteroid injections widely, and trials of injections for shoulder, tendon and joint conditions exist, though these concern other tissues [11][12].

Corticosteroid medicine began with cortisone in 1948 and hydrocortisone in 1951, and the 1950 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Edward Kendall, Tadeusz Reichstein and Philip Hench for work on adrenal hormones [6]. Triamcinolone and methylprednisolone followed in 1956, prednisone and prednisolone in 1955 and dexamethasone and betamethasone in 1958 [6]. Intralesional corticosteroids were first used as a scar treatment in the mid-1960s [4]. The US FDA approved triamcinolone acetonide as an over-the-counter nasal spray in 2014 [1].

Triamcinolone acetonide is the C16alpha,17alpha acetonide of triamcinolone. It acts as an agonist of the glucocorticoid receptor, with affinity for androgen and estrogen receptors below 0.1 percent of that of testosterone and estradiol, and it binds the progesterone receptor at about 15 percent of progesterone's affinity [1]. It is metabolised in the liver and excreted about 75 percent in urine and 25 percent in feces [1].

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation by blocking inflammatory mediators and inducing anti-inflammatory ones, and by suppressing T-cell driven reactions [6]. Placing the drug in the lesion is the rationale for local rather than systemic dosing [1]. In topical form triamcinolone acetonide sits in US potency class III at 0.5 percent, class IV at 0.1 percent and class VI at 0.025 percent, a moderate potency; hydrocortisone is a low-potency steroid sold over the counter in most countries [13][14].

Wikipedia notes that triamcinolone used for macular edema may raise intraocular pressure and that, because of progesterone receptor binding, it can inhibit ovulation and cause menstrual irregularity [1]. Ophthalmic studies of intravitreal triamcinolone report raised eye pressure (in one case series of 89 patients, a mean pressure change of 8.0 mm Hg) and, rarely, endophthalmitis [15][16]. These findings concern injection into the eye and are not studies of skin injection.

For the skin, Wikipedia's topical steroid article describes skin thinning with prolonged continuous use, visible small vessels, bruising and fragility, and perioral dermatitis, plus systemic effects such as adrenal suppression and raised eye pressure, and notes that tolerance can build within days [13]. Wikipedia's hydrocortisone article lists dose-dependent systemic effects including adrenal suppression and easy bruising with long-term use [14]. Corticosteroids in general are linked to hyperglycemia, infection risk, mood effects and osteoporosis at systemic exposure, and topical steroid withdrawal has been described after sudden discontinuation [6][13]. Wikipedia's keloid article says corticosteroids are not recommended for children because of risks such as growth effects [4].

Forum posters on T Nation who received corticosteroid injections for joint problems describe pain at the injection site and delayed relief, and one attributed hiccups to a shot, as personal reports [17].
No studies of intralesional corticosteroid injection of acne cysts were found.

Related registered studies of intralesional triamcinolone include a phase 2 study of Kenalog-10 in alopecia areata examining adrenal function (n=18) [9], a phase 2 study combining hyaluronic acid filler and triamcinolone for alopecia areata (n=14) [10], and a phase 4 trial of verapamil versus steroid to prevent keloid recurrence (terminated, n=14) [3]. The registry records cited do not report results. Wikipedia's alopecia areata article cites a 2020 systematic review in which more than half of treated patients had over 50 percent regrowth with triamcinolone injections, while cautioning that effectiveness is uncertain at some sites and that spontaneous regrowth complicates interpretation [5].

Studies in other tissues show how injections are evaluated elsewhere. A pragmatic randomised trial (GRASP) compared progressive exercise with best-practice advice, with or without corticosteroid injection, in rotator cuff disorders [11], and a randomised trial added ultrasound-guided corticosteroid or placebo injection to exercise for Achilles tendinopathy [12]. A case series of 15 patients tested a single intravitreal 4 mg triamcinolone injection for diabetic macular edema [18].

Discussion on looksmax.org centres on nose thinning through reduced soft-tissue swelling, framed by posters as experimental, with comparisons to hydrocortisone, isotretinoin and diuretics as other anti-inflammatory routes mentioned [7][8]. Posters describe their own results; no controlled data on this use are cited here.

Triamcinolone is prescription-only in most forms in the US, EU and UK, with status varying by country (for example scheduled in Australia and Canada, and listed as a banned race-day substance in horse racing) [1].

lore.intro: Triamcinolone appears on looksmax.org mostly in discussions of nose thinning, where members compare it with the weaker hydrocortisone [7][8]; injection into acne nodules is discussed in acne communities as a clinician-given quick fix.
